name: Seychelles
tagline: Granite islands in the Indian Ocean
summary: The only granite islands in the middle of an ocean anywhere on earth — Mahé, Praslin and La Digue, the coco de mer in the Vallée de Mai, and Aldabra's giant tortoises a thousand kilometres out.

entries.caption: Granite Islands in the Indian Ocean
entries.description: Ancient granite, not coral or volcano — these islands are a fragment of a broken continent.
entries.subject: granite boulders on a white beach at La Digue

entries.caption: Forty-Three Granite Islands
entries.description: Granite in the inner islands, coral atolls in the outer, and a thousand kilometres between.
entries.subject: the granite peaks of Mahé above the sea

entries.caption: Endemic Everywhere
entries.description: The black parrot, the magpie robin, and giant tortoises that live free on Curieuse.
entries.subject: a giant tortoise walking a beach on Curieuse

entries.caption: Not a Safari, a Reef
entries.description: The game here is under the water — reef fish, turtle, and whale shark off Mahé in season.
entries.subject: a green turtle over reef in clear water

entries.caption: Morne Seychellois
entries.description: Nine hundred metres of forested granite above Victoria, with trails through the mist forest.
entries.subject: the forested ridge of Morne Seychellois

entries.caption: Sauzier and the Streams
entries.description: Short granite streams off the ridges, and the Sauzier falls in the west of Mahé.
entries.subject: a stream falling over granite through forest on Mahé

entries.caption: No Rivers, All Sea
entries.description: The water here is the Indian Ocean, and the lagoons inside the reef.
entries.subject: the shallow lagoon inside a Seychelles reef

entries.caption: Anse Source d'Argent
entries.description: The most photographed beach in the world, and the granite is the reason why.
entries.subject: granite boulders and shallow water at Anse Source d'Argent

entries.caption: The Vallée de Mai
entries.description: Coco de mer palms in a valley on Praslin, and the largest seed of any plant on earth.
entries.subject: coco de mer palms in the Vallée de Mai

entries.caption: Dive, Sail, Walk
entries.description: Diving the granite drop-offs, sailing the inner islands, and walking Mahé's ridge trails.
entries.subject: a yacht anchored between granite islands

entries.caption: Creole
entries.description: African, French, Indian and Chinese, in one Creole language and one kitchen.
entries.subject: a Creole house with a wide veranda on Mahé

entries.caption: Island Life
entries.description: A hundred thousand people across a hundred and fifteen islands, most on three of them.
entries.subject: fishermen bringing in a catch at a Mahé jetty

entries.caption: Fish, Coconut and Chilli
entries.description: Grilled fish, coconut curry, breadfruit, and a chilli sauce that is not a suggestion.
entries.subject: grilled fish with coconut curry and rice

entries.caption: Festival Kreol
entries.description: Festival Kreol in October, and the sega and moutya danced through it.
entries.subject: dancers at the Festival Kreol on Mahé

entries.caption: Boatbuilding and Weaving
entries.description: Pirogue building on La Digue, and coconut palm weaving still done by hand.
entries.subject: a wooden pirogue being built on a beach

entries.caption: The Plantations
entries.description: L'Union Estate on La Digue, with its vanilla, copra mill and colonial house.
entries.subject: the copra mill and plantation house at L'Union Estate

entries.caption: Aldabra
entries.description: A thousand kilometres out, with a hundred thousand giant tortoises and almost no people.
entries.subject: the raised coral rim of the Aldabra atoll

entries.caption: Victoria
entries.description: One of the smallest capitals in the world, with a clock tower and a market.
entries.subject: the market and clock tower in Victoria, Mahé

entries.caption: Creole Houses
entries.description: Steep roofs, wide verandas and louvres — built for heat before anyone had a choice.
entries.subject: a traditional Creole house with louvred shutters

entries.caption: The Fish Market
entries.description: Victoria's market at eight in the morning is the most useful hour on the island.
entries.subject: the fish market in Victoria early in the morning

entries.caption: Shallow, Warm, Safe
entries.description: Lagoons inside the reef, no dangerous surf on most beaches, and short boat rides.
entries.subject: children in a shallow turquoise lagoon

entries.caption: Dive, Kayak, Cycle
entries.description: Granite dive sites, kayaks in the lagoons, and La Digue where the bicycle is the transport.
entries.subject: bicycles on a sandy track on La Digue

entries.caption: The Private Islands
entries.description: North Island, Frégate and Denis — private islands with a dozen villas on each.
entries.subject: a villa above a beach on a private Seychelles island

entries.caption: Half the Country Is Protected
entries.description: Forty-two per cent of the land is national park, and the marine parks now match it.
entries.subject: a marine park marker buoy over Seychelles reef

entries.caption: Granite and Turquoise
entries.description: Grey granite, white sand and three shades of blue — the reason every camera comes here.
entries.subject: granite boulders and turquoise water at sunset

entries.caption: La Digue by Bicycle
entries.description: No real roads and few cars — an island best measured in bicycle hours.
entries.subject: a sandy lane and bicycles under palms on La Digue

entries.caption: Nowhere Else Is Built Like This
entries.description: Granite in mid-ocean, a palm that grows nowhere else, and tortoises older than the state.
entries.subject: granite peaks and palms above a Seychelles beach
